title: The Future of School Is Tech-Intentional
author: Emily Cherkin
summary: Emily Cherkin recounts her keynote address at Manhattan Day School, which she identifies as the world's first Tech-Intentional Certified school, using the occasion to articulate the full theoretical and practical frame behind tech-intentional education. She diagnoses three simultaneous crises in American childhood that share a common root: a creativity crisis (children who cannot pretend to fly because imaginative capacity has been colonized by passive consumption), a learning crisis (NAEP scores declining, which she links to screentime displacing the cognitive work reading and open-ended play develop), and a mental health crisis (one in three teenage girls contemplated suicide in 2023). Cherkin argues that EdTech is structurally identical to Big Tech but wears a sweater vest: the same persuasive design techniques, infinite-scroll mechanics, and dopamine-driven engagement loops are built into classroom platforms, only now rebranded as personalized learning and twenty-first-century skills. The practical alternative she advocates is an analog-first childhood as the best preparation for a digital future -- children who have built robust imaginative, relational, and attentional capacity are better equipped to use technology as a tool rather than be used by it. Four principles of a tech-intentional school are identified: intentionality over default adoption, human connection before device mediation, developmentally appropriate tool use rather than age-agnostic deployment, and adult modeling of the device relationships we ask of children.
points: Three simultaneous crises -- creativity, learning, and mental health -- share a structural cause: technology deployment has displaced the developmental experiences (play, reading, embodied social interaction) that build those capacities.

EdTech is Big Tech in a sweater vest: the same persuasive-design mechanics that power social media are built into classroom platforms, rebranded as personalized learning rather than engagement maximization.
One in three teenage girls contemplated suicide in 2023 -- this is a public health emergency whose timing correlates precisely with smartphone ubiquity and social-media adolescence.

An analog-first childhood is the best preparation for a digital future: children who develop robust imaginative, attentional, and relational capacity are equipped to use technology as a tool rather than be used by it.

Tech-intentionality is not anti-technology; it is a commitment to asking 'Does this technology serve the child's development?' before deployment rather than adopting by default and mitigating harms retroactively.
quotes: I asked a room of kindergartners if they could pretend to fly. Half of them looked at me blankly. These are five-year-olds. Imagination is not a nice-to-have developmental outcome. It is the foundation of creativity, empathy, and the kind of flexible thinking no AI will replicate.

EdTech is Big Tech in a sweater vest. The same engineers who designed infinite scroll and variable reward loops for Instagram designed the classroom platforms we are currently calling personalized learning. The goals are identical: maximize time on platform.

One in three teenage girls contemplated suicide in 2023. We do not get to call this a mental health crisis and then hand sixth graders a device with the same persuasive architecture that drove those numbers.

An analog-first childhood is not a Luddite childhood. It is a developmental argument: the child who has spent years building imaginative, relational, and attentional capacity will be a far more capable technology user at fifteen than the child who was handed a device at eight.

Tech-intentional does not mean tech-free. It means we ask the developmental question first: Does this tool serve this child at this stage? That question changes almost every default decision schools are currently making.
